records.question: Under what conditions does the new fused dequantization path get disabled in favor of the older per-request behavior?
records.question_clean: Under what conditions does the new fused dequantization path get disabled in favor of the older per-request behavior?

perf: cross-batch dequant fusion with amortized per-token rescale for mixed-precision kernels

Motivation: Long-context workloads show fragmentation across microbatches that prevent effective dequant fusion and cause repeated dequant/rescale operations per token.

This PR introduces a cross-batch dequant fusion pass plus an amortized per-token rescale step that cooperates with the KV cache and continuous batching coordinator to reduce redundant dequant work for INT8/FP8 mixed-precision serving.\n\nSummary of changes: implemented a new CrossBatchDequanter that tracks compatible contiguous microbatch windows and emits a fused dequant operation for stacked tokens; added an AmortizedRescale operator that defers fine-grained scale adjustments until token groups exceed a stability threshold; extended the scheduler with a cross-batch affinity hint and modified the KV cache interface to expose per-layer scale metadata needed by the fused path.

Also added kernel-level fastpaths for fused int8->fp16 conversion targeting long prefix reuse patterns.\n\nDesign notes: the fused path is opt-in behind a runtime feature flag (RUNTIME_FUSED_DEQUANT).

When enabled the scheduler annotates queued requests with batch-affinity tags; CrossBatchDequanter periodically probes the queue to form mergeable windows constrained by latency SLO heuristics.

AmortizedRescale computes a combined scale factor and only applies per-token micro-adjustments when the cumulative quantization error crosses a configurable threshold (defaults tuned from benchmarks).

Compatibility: falls back to existing per-request dequant for heterogeneous model variants and when KV cache indicates incompatible scale signatures.\n\nBenchmarks: microbench on p4d.24xlarge with a 16k context evaluation harness showed up to 22% throughput improvement and 18% average token-latency reduction on customer-like chat load (95th percentile latency remained within SLO).

FP8/INT8 combined workloads saw better utilization due to fewer kernel launches and improved KV cache hit patterns.

Detailed numbers included in /docs/perf/crossbatch-dequant-run-2026-02-20.md.\n\nTesting: unit tests for CrossBatchDequanter and AmortizedRescale (kernel emulation mode), end-to-end CI smoke against the runtime with synthetic traffic, and a canary rollout configuration for Dedicated.

Stress tests included kv-cache warm/cold cycles and continuous-batching scenarios.

records.question: How does the new service-scoped KMS protection decide whether a principal can use a key, and what happens if the request is not allowed?
records.question_clean: How does the new service-scoped KMS protection decide whether a principal can use a key, and what happens if the request is not allowed?
records.gold_answer: Keys can be tagged with an optional service identifier when they are created. If a key has that binding, only principals whose service claim matches the key’s service binding, or principals explicitly listed as exceptions, may perform wrap, unwrap, or other key-usage actions. Requests that violate the binding are rejected immediately with HTTP 403 and the structured error code "kms.service_bound".
gold_chunks_text:
Add service-scoped KMS guardrails and audit ingestion harmonizer

Motivation: Customers operating multiple logical services under the same tenant require strict guarantees that service-A cannot request or unwrap keys bound to service-B. Incidents surfaced during an internal postmortem showed ambiguous key attribution for cross-service operator actions which complicates audits and violates customer isolation promises. This PR implements service-scoped KMS guardrails and a lightweight audit ingestion harmonizer to make audit events canonical and to prevent cross-service key usage by default.

What this PR does (high level): Adds a new enforcement middleware (kms/service-guard) that validates the requesting principal's service claim against the requested key's service binding. Introduces a new policy API to bind keys to a service identifier and to define an exception allowlist for operator flows. Adds an audit-ingestor microservice that normalizes incoming audit records, deduplicates identical events within a short window, enriches events with residency and key binding metadata, and forwards to the existing audit pipeline. Provides a backfill migration to tag historical events with best-effort service_kms_id and residency_claim (logged separately for traceability).

Design notes: - Service binding model: keys have an optional service_id tag set at creation time. When present, only principals with matching service_id or explicit allowlist entries may perform wrap/unwrap or key usage actions. The enforcement is opt-in for existing keys (to avoid breaking legacy customers); new keys have binding encouraged by CLI/console UX. - Failure modes: requests that violate binding fail early with 403 and an structured error code kms.service_bound. Operator-level exceptions can be granted via RBAC role "kms:service-bypass" which requires multi-approver escalation (see RBAC section). - Audit harmonization: the ingestor normalizes heterogenous audit sources (gateway, kms-proxy, operator-proxy) into a canonical event schema (timestamp, principal, service_id, kms_key_id, op, residency_claim, request_id, provenance_chain). It also deduplicates retry storms within a 30s window to reduce noise in retention stores. - Backward compatibility: enforcement for existing keys is behind a feature flag enforcement.kms.service_bind and rollout uses a canary cohort. The ingestor will accept both legacy and canonical payloads and will write a normalized event alongside the original raw event for troubleshooting.

intent_points.text: A key may have an optional service identifier binding/tag set at creation time.
When a key is service-bound, only principals with a matching service claim or an explicit allowlist/exception entry may use it for wrap/unwrap or key usage operations.
If the binding check fails, the request is denied early with HTTP 403 and the error code "kms.service_bound".

Document KMS error taxonomy in code and logs

## Summary
This PR adds inline documentation and concrete conventions for how we represent KMS failures in logs and traces. The goal is to make triage consistent across services (control plane + data plane) and to ensure dashboards/alerts can rely on stable field names.

This is intentionally “docs + conventions + guardrails”, not functional behavior changes. It complements the wrapper work in pr-18421 and metrics/spans work in pr-18434.

Linked: ENG-4822 (taxonomy + metrics tags), ENG-4823 (wrapper).

## What changed
- Adds a canonical KMS error taxonomy enum (with mapping notes) and documents when each category is used.
- Defines structured log field names + required fields for all KMS failures.
- Documents how errors should be surfaced to operators (what’s safe to include, what must be redacted).
- Adds a small helper that ensures required KMS log fields are present when logging wrapper errors (compile-time references + unit tests).

## Canonical taxonomy (required)
When a KMS operation fails, the wrapper MUST map to one of these kinds:
- `AccessDenied` (IAM/principal/key policy; includes `kms:Decrypt` denied)
- `NotFound` (key ARN/id not found, alias missing)
- `Throttling` (rate exceeded / quota)
- `Timeout` (client-side deadline, upstream hang)
- `InvalidCiphertext` (decrypt fails due to wrong key/material mismatch)
- `KeyDisabled` (key disabled/pending deletion)
- `DependencyUnavailable` (upstream service error/outage; retryable)
- `Unknown` (fallback bucket; should be rare and triggers follow-up)

Notes:
- We explicitly separate `Timeout` from `DependencyUnavailable` to support the retry-budget and circuit breaker policy work.
- `InvalidCiphertext` is treated as non-retryable by default; operationally it’s typically a mismatch (wrong key id/version, stale cache, bad ciphertext).

tooling/execution: concurrency safeguards and tool-result-injection ergonomics

Motivation: Customers integrating complex tool chains reported flaky outputs when multiple tools ran in parallel and tool results were injected back into the model stream.

This PR standardizes execution semantics for multi-tool calls, adds runtime safeguards for parallelism, and harmonizes behavior with our OpenAI-compat surface.

Summary of changes: 1) Executor: introduce a per-request "tool-parallelism" cap (configurable at API/route level) that bounds concurrent tool invocations and provides backpressure hooks to the scheduler; 2) Injection protocol: formalize a deterministic injection ordering when multiple tool results arrive within the same model turn and attach an idempotency token to each injected result so retries do not duplicate content; 3) Retry semantics: new retry policy enum (none, best-effort, strict-idempotent) exposed via the API and respected by the runtime and OpenAI-compat shim; 4) Streaming stability: when streaming responses include tool-calls, we now atomically flush tool-invocation markers to the stream and gracefully resume generation once injected results are committed to the KV cache; 5) OpenAI-compat updates: function-calling payloads now accept an optional "execution_hints" map with parallelism and idempotency hints that the compat layer translates into our internal routing and executor options; 6) Observability: emit new metrics (tool.invocations.active, tool.invocations.queued, tool.injection.latency) and traces annotated with execution_hints for easier debugging.

Implementation notes: - Executor changes are confined to runtime/executor/* and api/handlers/tool_call_handler.go; the executor preserves the previous scheduling algorithm but applies per-request parallelism caps before dispatching tool workers. - Injection order uses a deterministic comparator: (request_tool_sequence, tool_priority, start_timestamp).

This avoids nondeterministic interleaving in model-visible outputs. - Idempotency tokens are short-lived UUIDs persisted in the request context and kept in the per-request token-cache; replayed tool results with matching token are ignored by the injection layer. - The OpenAI compatibility shim accepts additional fields but falls back to previous behavior when execution_hints are omitted to preserve backward compatibility.

Interleaved activation checkpointing and buffer coalescing to cut peak GPU workspace

Motivation: In production we observed recurring OOMs and large transient workspace peaks for long-sequence (>=4k) generation and KV-heavy batched workloads. Previous work focused on per-layer checkpointing and arena sizing; this PR targets three complementary levers to reduce peak GPU footprint without changing numeric behavior: 1) interleaved activation checkpointing that staggers recompute windows to shrink concurrent activation sets, 2) scratch buffer coalescing that merges short-lived per-op scratch allocations into a reusable sub-arena, and 3) scheduler hints that adjust continuous-batching flush thresholds to avoid pathological peak overlaps with KV cache refill phases.

- commit 1: implement interleaved checkpoint planner and unit tests (planner/ckpt_planner.{cpp,h}, tests/ckpt_planner_tests.cpp)
- commit 2: introduce coalesced scratch allocator and sub-arena lifecycle (runtime/scratch_coalesce.{cpp,h}, runtime/sub_arena.{cpp,h})
- commit 3: hook allocator into kernel queue; add allocator metrics and tracing points (runtime/kernel_queue.cpp, observability/metrics_registry.cpp)
- commit 4: scheduler hint API and continuous-batching adjustments (scheduler/flush_policy.{cpp,h}, api/scheduler_config.md)
- commit 5: perf harness & benchmarks (perf/bench_long_seq.py, perf/bench_report_24678.md)
- commit 6: address review comments, test flakiness fixes, additional microbenchmarks (various)

atomic release staging, Helm preflight hooks, and compressed release manifests for safer private-installer rollouts

Motivation: private on‑prem/VPC upgrades require greater atomicity and preflight validation to avoid partial rollouts and long rollback windows.

This PR introduces a small release staging layer, Helm preflight hooks (pre-install/pre-upgrade/validate), and a compact compression/packing step for release manifests and provenance files so that the installer can stage an entire release snapshot atomically and validate it before switching the live release pointer.

Design summary: 1) release-stager: an ephemeral staging area in S3/GCS with an atomic 'active' pointer object; publish pipeline uploads a packed, signed archive and a JSON index; after successful post-signature validations the pipeline atomically swaps a symlink-style object (bucket key replace) to make the new release active; 2) manifest packing: index_pack.go creates deterministic tar stream, zstd compresses blobs with level 3 for speed, and the pack includes SHA256 provenance metadata for each entry to simplify verification during installs; 3) Helm preflight hooks: small Helm hooks run before install/upgrade to validate node resources, image accessibility, KMS availability, and required CRDs; failures are surfaced early and abort the Helm transaction; 4) installer/rollback: upgrade tool gains a two-phase apply with an automatic dry-run validation and a deterministic rollback plan derived from the staged index so rollbacks are fast and do not rely on ad-hoc heuristics.

## Summary
This PR adds inline documentation and concrete conventions for how we represent KMS failures in logs and traces. The goal is to make triage consistent across services (control plane + data plane) and to ensure dashboards/alerts can rely on stable field names.

This is intentionally “docs + conventions + guardrails”, not functional behavior changes. It complements the wrapper work in pr-18421 and metrics/spans work in pr-18434.

Linked: ENG-4822 (taxonomy + metrics tags), ENG-4823 (wrapper).

## What changed
- Adds a canonical KMS error taxonomy enum (with mapping notes) and documents when each category is used.
- Defines structured log field names + required fields for all KMS failures.
- Documents how errors should be surfaced to operators (what’s safe to include, what must be redacted).
- Adds a small helper that ensures required KMS log fields are present when logging wrapper errors (compile-time references + unit tests).

## Canonical taxonomy (required)
When a KMS operation fails, the wrapper MUST map to one of these kinds:
- `AccessDenied` (IAM/principal/key policy; includes `kms:Decrypt` denied)
- `NotFound` (key ARN/id not found, alias missing)
- `Throttling` (rate exceeded / quota)
- `Timeout` (client-side deadline, upstream hang)
- `InvalidCiphertext` (decrypt fails due to wrong key/material mismatch)
- `KeyDisabled` (key disabled/pending deletion)
- `DependencyUnavailable` (upstream service error/outage; retryable)
- `Unknown` (fallback bucket; should be rare and triggers follow-up)

Notes:
- We explicitly separate `Timeout` from `DependencyUnavailable` to support the retry-budget and circuit breaker policy work.
- `InvalidCiphertext` is treated as non-retryable by default; operationally it’s typically a mismatch (wrong key id/version, stale cache, bad ciphertext).

Signed Terraform Plan Artifacts and Helm-diff Rollback Gating

Context and motivation:
This PR implements a reproducible, signed artifact workflow for Terraform plans and a Helm-chart-diff-driven rollback gating mechanism for the private installer CI/CD. Recent customer upgrades highlighted two operational gaps: (1) lack of a verifiable plan artifact to attest exactly what will change during an upgrade, and (2) upgrades failing to generate deterministic rollback anchors when chart/value drift occurs in airgapped environments.

Summary of changes:
- Generate a canonical, reproducible terraform plan JSON during staging, canonicalize it (strip timestamps, sort maps), and sign the blob with cosign using the org KMS key. Signed artifacts are uploaded to the release bucket under /plans/<release>/<cluster>.plan.json.sig and recorded in the release manifest.
- Add a lightweight plan-verifier binary (tools/plan-verifier) used in CI and in the installer preflight to validate signatures and ensure the on-cluster state matches the plan fingerprint before applying.
- Add a Helm chart diff preflight that computes a normalized diff between current deployed chart+values and the candidate release, identifies changed template keys that are rollback-risky (stateful migration hooks, volume changes), and produces a rollback anchor entry to include in the release manifest.
- CI: new pipeline step ci/pipelines/verify-signed-plan.yml to gate merges for private-installer changes that touch upgrade paths. The pipeline verifies signatures, runs the helm-diff preflight against a live staging cluster simulator, and publishes the artifacts.
- Docs: docs/upgrade-runbook.md extended with a signed-plan troubleshooting section and instructions for on-prem operators on how to rotate signing keys.

Design notes and security posture:
- Artifact signing uses cosign with KMS-backed keys (AWS KMS / GCP KMS interchangeable). The plan JSON canonicalization is intentionally strict: deterministic ordering of resources and consistent provider addresses to ensure reproducible fingerprinting across CI runs.
- The plan artifact and helm-diff anchor are stored with provenance metadata (git ref, pipeline id, signer id) and included in the release manifest so the installer can make allowlist decisions during an airgapped apply.
- The preflight runs in two modes: CI-mode (simulator) and runtime-mode (installer preflight). The latter defaults to fail-closed when signatures or anchors are absent, but an operator flag --allow-unsigned-upgrades is available for troubleshooting with audit logging.

Add service-scoped KMS guardrails and audit ingestion harmonizer

Motivation: Customers operating multiple logical services under the same tenant require strict guarantees that service-A cannot request or unwrap keys bound to service-B. Incidents surfaced during an internal postmortem showed ambiguous key attribution for cross-service operator actions which complicates audits and violates customer isolation promises. This PR implements service-scoped KMS guardrails and a lightweight audit ingestion harmonizer to make audit events canonical and to prevent cross-service key usage by default.

What this PR does (high level): Adds a new enforcement middleware (kms/service-guard) that validates the requesting principal's service claim against the requested key's service binding. Introduces a new policy API to bind keys to a service identifier and to define an exception allowlist for operator flows. Adds an audit-ingestor microservice that normalizes incoming audit records, deduplicates identical events within a short window, enriches events with residency and key binding metadata, and forwards to the existing audit pipeline. Provides a backfill migration to tag historical events with best-effort service_kms_id and residency_claim (logged separately for traceability).

Design notes: - Service binding model: keys have an optional service_id tag set at creation time. When present, only principals with matching service_id or explicit allowlist entries may perform wrap/unwrap or key usage actions. The enforcement is opt-in for existing keys (to avoid breaking legacy customers); new keys have binding encouraged by CLI/console UX. - Failure modes: requests that violate binding fail early with 403 and an structured error code kms.service_bound. Operator-level exceptions can be granted via RBAC role "kms:service-bypass" which requires multi-approver escalation (see RBAC section). - Audit harmonization: the ingestor normalizes heterogenous audit sources (gateway, kms-proxy, operator-proxy) into a canonical event schema (timestamp, principal, service_id, kms_key_id, op, residency_claim, request_id, provenance_chain). It also deduplicates retry storms within a 30s window to reduce noise in retention stores. - Backward compatibility: enforcement for existing keys is behind a feature flag enforcement.kms.service_bind and rollout uses a canary cohort. The ingestor will accept both legacy and canonical payloads and will write a normalized event alongside the original raw event for troubleshooting.

Changed areas (representative): - core/kms/middleware/service_guard.go: new enforcement middleware and policy evaluator - api/kms/policy.go: API surface to bind keys and query service bindings - services/audit/ingestor/*: new service that normalizes, dedupes, enriches audit events and forwards to kafka/topic audit.normalized - infra/eks/manifests/audit-ingestor.yaml: k8s manifest and RBAC for the ingestor - tools/migrations/20241112_backfill_service_kms_tags.go: migration to tag historical events - docs/security/kms-service-binding.md: runbook and operator guidance - tests/e2e/kms_service_binding_test.go and unit tests across middleware/ingestor

Testing and verification: - Unit tests cover policy evaluation matrix, denial messages, and the fallback path for unbound keys. - Integration tests run a mini-ingestor and replayed audit payloads validating normalization and dedupe behavior. - E2E smoke includes creation of bound key, attempt to use key with non-matching service principal (expect 403), and operator unbind flow (requires role and audit note). - CI: lint, unit, integration, and e2e stages passed on the merge run (flaky test t-queue-429 retried once).

Migration and rollout plan: - Phase 1 (canary): enable audit-ingestor in staging and wire a 5% subset of production traffic for 48h. Run backfill in read-only mode to evaluate heuristics. - Phase 2 (soft enforcement): enable service_bind enforcement for newly-created keys and opt-in existing keys via console prompts. Run with monitoring dashboards for reject rate and false positives. - Phase 3 (enforce for cohort): enable enforcement for a subset of tenants that opted-in; continue backfill and provide operator tooling to request exception. - Phase 4 (global): flip enforcement.kms.service_bind and promote ingestor as primary audit-normalizer.

Rollout guards and SLOs: - Alert if reject rate for bound-key usage > 0.1% of normal traffic for 1h and if normalized audit ingest latency > 500ms p95. - Provide a rollback flag to disable enforcement cluster-wide within 15 minutes.

Commitment gap auditor and rollback impact simulator

Add a runtime auditor that detects divergence between committed tenant throughput and observed delivery; include a rollback impact simulator and operator-facing visualization to validate safe decommit scenarios.

Context: Dedicated customers buy committed throughput and we must ensure the fleet honors commitments and can safely decommit/reschedule capacity when required.

Motivation: recent support cases exposed hard-to-reproduce gaps between committed units and delivered throughput under bursty demand and transient preemptions.

This PR adds a Commitment Gap Auditor service that continuously compares contract-level commitments to recent delivery (p50/p95 throughput and admission failures), and a deterministic Rollback Impact Simulator that lets operators run 'what-if' decommit scenarios against a sliding-window utilization model.

Summary of changes: - new long-running service `commitment-auditor` (controller + API) that samples per-tenant reservation ledgers and emits gap alerts and suggested mitigations - a simulator binary (`rollback-sim`) that replays recent activity to estimate percent of tenant requests that would have been throttled under candidate decommit plans - operator UI endpoints (JSON + CSV) to fetch simulated outcomes and a small Prometheus metrics set for alerting - lightweight safety guards: automatic soft-hold when a decommit would cause >5% of active requests to regress past SLO for 5m - e2e tests and an integration scenario based test harness to reproduce regression locally Checklist: - [x] design doc (docs/design/commitment-auditor.md) - [x] unit & integration tests - [x] metrics + alert rules (basic) - [x] minimal operator UI endpoints - [x] rollout plan discussed with SRE and Sales Impact: This is an operator-facing feature that does not change runtime scheduling by default.

New service runs as opt-in; default is disabled in Dedicated clusters until we complete a controlled rollout.

Add structured output example + JSON schema validation helper (Go)

Context: Support + Solutions Eng have repeatedly flagged that customers copy/paste a structured-output snippet, immediately hit JSON parse/validation errors, and then have no idea what the “safe” handling path is (SUP-18436). This PR adds a runnable Go example that demonstrates schema-constrained output, safe parsing/validation, and a pragmatic fallback/retry strategy. It also updates doc comments in the SDK to align terminology with the docs refresh ("structured output" / "schema-constrained"), and to warn against incremental JSON parsing during streaming.

What’s included: 1) New runnable example: examples/structured_output_jsonschema/main.go - Requests schema-constrained output from the model - Collects the final assistant message before parsing (no incremental parse) - Validates against a JSON Schema (type/required/additionalProperties) - On validation failure: logs a compact error, retries once with a tighter system message, then falls back to non-structured extraction 2) Lightweight validation helper (example-scoped): examples/internal/jsonschema/validate.go - Uses github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v5 to compile/validate a schema string - Returns a single error string suitable for end-user logs (keeps example output clean) 3) Doc comment updates: - client/response types: clarify that “structured output” is best-effort across models and should be validated - streaming notes: explicitly recommend assembling the final message before parsing JSON

Example schema used in the sample: The example constrains output to an object with required fields and no additional properties: {"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,"required":["title","priority","due_date"],"properties":{"title":{"type":"string","minLength":1},"priority":{"type":"string","enum":["low","medium","high"]},"due_date":{"type":"string","pattern":"^\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}$"}}}

User-visible behavior: Running the example prints a validated struct on success; on failure it prints a single-line validation error plus the raw model output (truncated to 1KB) for debugging.

Add idiomatic retry presets and lightweight stream control across Python/TypeScript/Go SDKs

Motivation: We have accumulated several ad-hoc retry/backoff variants across SDKs and inconsistent streaming cancellation ergonomics.

This PR introduces a small, opinionated set of language-idiomatic retry presets plus a lightweight stream control surface (cancel token + backpressure hint hook) implemented consistently in Python, TypeScript, and Go.

Goals: 1) Provide three vetted presets (optimistic, balanced, conservative) for common production workloads so teams can pick sensible defaults without tuning; 2) Add a streaming control hook that surfaces a cancel token and an optional onBackpressure callback for consumer-driven pacing; 3) Keep implementations idiomatic per language (async context manager for Python, AbortSignal-friendly for TS, context.Context integration for Go); 4) Bump SDK minor versions and update changelogs and docs.

Compatibility: Presets are opt-in; default behavior is unchanged unless a preset or config is supplied.

Horizon-driven kernel activation and pulse flush controller for more stable streaming TTFB

Context / motivation: Streaming-first-byte latency (TTFB) for short, interactive LLM sessions remains noisy under mixed workloads. Prior work improved emitter tick pacing and KV prefetching, but we still observe sporadic 100-300ms spikes when kernels are cold or competing microbatches collide. This PR introduces two complementary runtime mechanisms: (1) a horizon-driven kernel activation heuristic that proactively brings up kernel execution contexts based on a compact prefix horizon prediction, and (2) a pulse flush controller that shapes flush cadence as a function of outstanding credits, kernel activation state, and observed downstream ACK latency. Together these reduce tail TTFB without increasing steady-state token-cost.

What this change does (single continuous description): Implements a lightweight KernelHorizon predictor that consumes per-request prefix length, recent token issuance rate, and model-config microprofile to compute a short horizon window (in tokens) that is likely to be requested within the next emission cycle. The KernelManager uses the horizon to start kernel activation (allocate workspace, populate sparse KV slices, pin working set) ahead of inevitable demand. Activation uses a low-overhead fast-path that avoids heavy warmup if prediction confidence is low. The PulseFlushController coordinates flush decisions: instead of a fixed tick or credit drain, the controller emits a flush pulse when (a) the current emitter microbatch is above a dynamic urgency threshold, (b) kernel activation readiness crosses confidence threshold, or (c) a deadline slack indicates we must send partial output to meet SLO. The pulse controller also feeds back to the request-level credit allocator to temporarily increase credits for streams that triggered kernel activation, preventing self-inflicted head-of-line blocking. The feature is behind a runtime feature flag (runtime.streaming.horizon_activation=true) and gated by an experiment rollout that uses per-pod sampling and progressive ramp to 100%.

Engineering notes: The KernelHorizon predictor is intentionally conservative: it prefers under-predicting to avoid unnecessary memory pressure. It uses a short exponential moving average on inter-token intervals with model-config priors (max generation length, typical chunk sizes). Activation state machines are idempotent and cancelable; if the horizon estimate changes, activation can be deescalated to a low-power hold. PulseFlushController uses a leaky-bucket-style urgency accumulator with hysteresis to avoid oscillation under variable network ACKs. We record new metrics (runtime.kernel_horizon.confidence, runtime.kernel_activation.latency_ms, runtime.pulse_flush.count, runtime.pulse_flush.reason) and propagate them to tracing spans for waterfall analysis.

Performance summary: Bench results on q4-small (gpt-small-ish) workloads with mixed short chats and long completions: median TTFB improved 12%, p95 improved 18%, p99 improved 13% while token throughput remained within 1% loss. In microbench synthetic cold-start tests, the mean activation latency is 45ms (90ms 95th) with horizon pre-activation vs 170ms cold latency baseline. Cost impact: slight increase in transient memory allocations during activation windows (approx +2% GPU memory footprint on average for mixed workloads) but no measurable increase in per-token compute cost.

Compatibility & safety: Feature is disabled by default. Fallback behavior: if KernelManager cannot allocate activation resources within a short timeout, the pulse controller will revert to conservative flush cadence to prevent latency regressions. We added a kill-switch at pod-level to disable horizon activation in-flight. No API surface changes.

Testing: Unit tests for the KernelHorizon prediction logic and state machine, integration streaming tests that simulate varying ACK latencies and workload mixes, and an end-to-end perf harness run. Added deterministic replay tests to ensure activation cancellation doesn't leak resources. See tests/stream_perf_integration_test.py for scenarios.

Rollout plan: start with 5% of streaming pods for 48h, monitor runtime.kernel_activation.latency_ms and runtime.pulse_flush.count, then 25% for 24h, and full ramp if no regressions. Post-merge follow-ups include adding model-specific horion priors for large-context decoders and a telemetry dashboard to correlate activation events with p99 TTFB.

Related work: builds on ENG-3128 emitter pacing improvements and complements previous KV-prefetch PRs by focusing activation timing rather than cache policy. Also ties into Observability tagging work (ENG-3201) to surface activation events in traces.

Document KMS error taxonomy in code and logs

## Summary
This PR adds inline documentation and concrete conventions for how we represent KMS failures in logs and traces. The goal is to make triage consistent across services (control plane + data plane) and to ensure dashboards/alerts can rely on stable field names.

This is intentionally “docs + conventions + guardrails”, not functional behavior changes. It complements the wrapper work in pr-18421 and metrics/spans work in pr-18434.

Linked: ENG-4822 (taxonomy + metrics tags), ENG-4823 (wrapper).

## What changed
- Adds a canonical KMS error taxonomy enum (with mapping notes) and documents when each category is used.
- Defines structured log field names + required fields for all KMS failures.
- Documents how errors should be surfaced to operators (what’s safe to include, what must be redacted).
- Adds a small helper that ensures required KMS log fields are present when logging wrapper errors (compile-time references + unit tests).

## Canonical taxonomy (required)
When a KMS operation fails, the wrapper MUST map to one of these kinds:
- `AccessDenied` (IAM/principal/key policy; includes `kms:Decrypt` denied)
- `NotFound` (key ARN/id not found, alias missing)
- `Throttling` (rate exceeded / quota)
- `Timeout` (client-side deadline, upstream hang)
- `InvalidCiphertext` (decrypt fails due to wrong key/material mismatch)
- `KeyDisabled` (key disabled/pending deletion)
- `DependencyUnavailable` (upstream service error/outage; retryable)
- `Unknown` (fallback bucket; should be rare and triggers follow-up)

Notes:
- We explicitly separate `Timeout` from `DependencyUnavailable` to support the retry-budget and circuit breaker policy work.
- `InvalidCiphertext` is treated as non-retryable by default; operationally it’s typically a mismatch (wrong key id/version, stale cache, bad ciphertext).

## Required log fields
All logs emitted for KMS failures MUST include:
- `kms.provider`: `aws|gcp|azure|other`
- `kms.operation`: `Encrypt|Decrypt|GenerateDataKey|DescribeKey|GetPublicKey|...`
- `kms.key_id`: stable logical identifier (redacted if customer policy requires; see below)
- `kms.key_arn`: when available; may be redacted/hashed in Private (configurable)
- `kms.region`
- `kms.request_id`: provider request id if available
- `kms.error.kind`: one of the canonical taxonomy values above
- `kms.error.code`: raw provider code (e.g., `AccessDeniedException`, `ThrottlingException`)
- `kms.http_status`: when available
- `kms.retryable`: `true|false`
- `kms.retry.count`: retry attempts executed for this request
- `kms.latency_ms`: end-to-end wrapper latency

Optional but recommended:
- `kms.circuit_breaker.state`: `closed|open|half_open`
- `kms.timeout_budget_ms`: configured deadline for the operation
- `kms.throttle`: `true|false` (alias for filtering; derived from kind/code)
- `trace_id` / `span_id` (already standard, but called out here because dashboards depend on it)

Redaction guidance:
- Never log plaintext, decrypted payloads, or DEK material.
- `kms.key_arn` may be considered sensitive for some Private customers; if `KMS_LOG_KEY_ARNS=false`, log a stable hash in `kms.key_arn_hash` and omit `kms.key_arn`.

kv: fine-grained age histograms and spill-horizon controller for low-fragmentation eviction

Introduces tenant-aware age histograms for KV cache and a Spill-Horizon controller that reduces unnecessary spill traffic under moderate pressure; improves tail latency and reduces write amplification during compaction.

Motivation: We observed recurring tail latency spikes and excess spill I/O on multi-tenant hosts during short-lived memory pressure bursts.

The current eviction logic is primarily LRU-like with coarse tenant quotas and lacks temporal fragmentation signal, which drives premature page spills and frequent small compactions.

This PR introduces two complementary subsystems: (1) fine-grained per-tenant age histograms (AgeBuckets) that produce a compact fragmentation/temperature fingerprint for each tenant, and (2) a Spill-Horizon controller that uses age distributions, recent spill latency, and global reservation headroom to delay or coalesce spill actions until an adaptive horizon is crossed.

Together they reduce unnecessary spill churn and make eviction decisions more locality- and age-aware.

Local stress ran with 64 tenants (mix of 90% cold / 10% hot distributions) for 30 minutes.

Compared to baseline main: - p50 eviction latency unchanged (~1.2ms), - p95 spill latency reduced 28%, - p99 spill rate (spills/sec) reduced 3.6x, - write amplification during compaction decreased 22%.

Memory overhead for AgeBuckets averaged +0.7% of heap on a 512GB node and stays bounded via sampling and caps.

Includes unit tests for histogram updates and spill-horizon backoff; integration test exercising deferred spills under fluctuating pressure; stress harness script to reproduce multi-tenant bursty workload.

Ran full test matrix (linux/cgo) and the new stress scenario in CI; e2e run in staging for 48h before merge.

Feature gated behind kv.experimental.age_histograms and kv.spill_horizon_enabled flags.

Default rollout is off for Dedicated until 2024-06-15, gradually enabled for 10% of hosted clusters, monitor spill_horizon_defer_total and compaction_write_bytes metrics before wider rollout.

consolidate-release-indexer-and-rollback-manifest-generator-for-private-installer

Introduce a single release indexer and rollback manifest generator for the private-installer packaging pipeline.

Motivation: current release metadata for private deployments is fragmented across per-arch Helm indexes, tarball lists, and ad-hoc rollback blobs which complicates automated upgrades and makes rollbacks error-prone.

This PR adds a deterministic release-index.json format that aggregates artifacts (helm charts, installer tarballs, OCI blobs), provenance pointers (cosign signatures, sbom hashes, attestation references) and a compact rollback-manifests/ directory with incremental patches used by the installer to perform atomic rollbacks.

Changes: - add cmd/release-indexer: builds release-index.json from CI artifacts, computes deterministic stable IDs, attaches provenance bundle references, and emits signed index + incremental patch files - add cmd/rollback-gen: produces rollback-manifests/<release>-<seq>.json that the installer uses to roll back a specific component set - update private-installer Helm chart values and templates to read release-index.json and prefer pinned artifact URLs when present - terraform/modules/s3-buckets: add new prefixing and lifecycle policy used to host both indexes and incremental patches - CI: new workflow .github/workflows/release-indexer.yml that runs indexer on build artifacts, cosigns the index, generates SBOM deltas, and publishes to release-buckets - docs: document index schema, upgrade flow, and rollback semantics - tests: unit tests for stable ID generation, e2e test that simulates an upgrade then verifies rollback-manifests apply cleanly Notes on implementation: the indexer computes stable IDs using a canonical JSON serialization and sha256 over (artifact URL, arch, variant, semantic version, builder-provenance).

The rollback-gen ensures patches are idempotent by using a three-way diff against the previous index and emitting reverse-apply steps.

tooling/execution: concurrency safeguards and tool-result-injection ergonomics

Motivation: Customers integrating complex tool chains reported flaky outputs when multiple tools ran in parallel and tool results were injected back into the model stream.

This PR standardizes execution semantics for multi-tool calls, adds runtime safeguards for parallelism, and harmonizes behavior with our OpenAI-compat surface.

Summary of changes: 1) Executor: introduce a per-request "tool-parallelism" cap (configurable at API/route level) that bounds concurrent tool invocations and provides backpressure hooks to the scheduler; 2) Injection protocol: formalize a deterministic injection ordering when multiple tool results arrive within the same model turn and attach an idempotency token to each injected result so retries do not duplicate content; 3) Retry semantics: new retry policy enum (none, best-effort, strict-idempotent) exposed via the API and respected by the runtime and OpenAI-compat shim; 4) Streaming stability: when streaming responses include tool-calls, we now atomically flush tool-invocation markers to the stream and gracefully resume generation once injected results are committed to the KV cache; 5) OpenAI-compat updates: function-calling payloads now accept an optional "execution_hints" map with parallelism and idempotency hints that the compat layer translates into our internal routing and executor options; 6) Observability: emit new metrics (tool.invocations.active, tool.invocations.queued, tool.injection.latency) and traces annotated with execution_hints for easier debugging.

Implementation notes: - Executor changes are confined to runtime/executor/* and api/handlers/tool_call_handler.go; the executor preserves the previous scheduling algorithm but applies per-request parallelism caps before dispatching tool workers. - Injection order uses a deterministic comparator: (request_tool_sequence, tool_priority, start_timestamp).

This avoids nondeterministic interleaving in model-visible outputs. - Idempotency tokens are short-lived UUIDs persisted in the request context and kept in the per-request token-cache; replayed tool results with matching token are ignored by the injection layer. - The OpenAI compatibility shim accepts additional fields but falls back to previous behavior when execution_hints are omitted to preserve backward compatibility.

The idempotency token approach requires minimal state but does not protect against cross-request duplicate side-effects (we call this out in the design doc).

jurisdictional-sink-orchestrator: idempotent reconciler + terraform module hooks for private installs

Motivation: Private installations running in multi-region VPCs need deterministic, auditable wiring of audit-log export sinks per jurisdiction and a reconciler that is safe to re-run during installer upgrades and rollbacks. Current behaviour relied on imperative hooks in the installer which caused drift when upgrades failed mid-flight and made it difficult to guarantee retention policies in cross-region setups. This PR introduces a jurisdiction-aware sink orchestration controller and wiring hooks for the private installer + Terraform modules so audit sinks are created and reconciled idempotently.

Summary of changes: 1) Add a small long-running reconciler (go controller) that watches AuditSink CRs and desired sink mapping from the installer; it performs create/update/delete with strong idempotency guarantees and emits detailed audit events (sink-reconciler.* metrics). 2) Extend terraform modules with new outputs and lifecycle-driven hooks so the private-installer can emit a desired-state manifest into the cluster (terraform/modules/audit_sink/*). 3) Helm chart changes: templates now include jurisdiction labels, retention annotations, and optional lifecycle hooks to defer reconciliation until KMS/secret rotation completes. 4) Installer: on the private-installer side we add a declarative sink-write step that applies the desired-state manifest and waits for the reconciler to report success; this replaces the previous ad-hoc shell provisioning. 5) Tests and e2e: add deterministic e2e that simulates mid-upgrade failures and validates rollback idempotency and retention enforcement.

Checklist: - [x] Controller implemented with retries and backoff, idempotent create/update path - [x] Terraform module hooks and docs added - [x] Helm templates updated for jurisdiction and retention annotations - [x] Installer wiring uses desired-state manifest for reconciliation - [x] Unit + e2e tests added and passing - [x] tfsec and helm linting addressed (one warning suppressed with justification)

Deployment notes: - This is backward compatible: the reconciler will adopt existing sinks by matching labels, so rollout can be done with a simple Canary (deploy reconciler -> enable terraform desired-state output -> flip installer to use manifest). - For air-gapped installs the reconciler image is included in the private registry bundle; ensure registry credentials are present prior to enabling the controller. - KMS-backed sinks: reconciler respects annotated kms_key_ref and will wait for secret readiness before finalizing sink wiring.

Rollback behavior: the reconciler is intentionally conservative: on deletion it removes only sink resources it created or owns (ownerReferences + managed-by label). If an installer rollback is triggered mid-upgrade, re-running the installer applies the same desired-state manifest and the reconciler converges back to the prior state without orphaning temporary resources.

Related work and references: Linear tickets ENG-2147 and ENG-2153 track the reconciler and terraform integrations. See internal design doc: https://linear.app/redwood/board/ENG-2147/jurisdictional-sink-orchestration and runbook: docs/private/audit-sink-orchestrator.md

Why this is different from previous PRs: previous changes focused on retention lifecycles and sink rotation; this change focuses on making sink wiring declarative and upgrade/rollback safe at the installer and terraform boundaries so compliance operators can guarantee retention and export topology after any control-plane operation.

Add deferred-indexing RAG playbook and streaming tool-proxy adapter

Summary: Adds a compact RAG playbook that demonstrates deferred (background) indexing semantics combined with a streaming tool-proxy adapter for tool-calls.

Motivation: many production RAG pipelines need to accept writes (ingestion) while keeping the serving index stable; fully reindexing synchronously is expensive and causes visible latency spikes.

This playbook shows a pragmatic pattern: 1) ingest -> enqueue -> optimistic-serve from a hot prefix cache; 2) background indexer that performs incremental merges and emits cleanup/metrics; 3) a streaming tool-proxy that forwards tool calls to external services via a websocket-backed relay and exposes a local replay hook for offline tests.

What this PR contains:
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/README.md: conceptual notes, sequence diagrams (ASCII) and runbook for tradeoffs.
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/docker-compose.yml: minimal local stack (producer, indexer, redis queue, preview server).
- playbooks/deferred-indexing/examples/ingest_client.py: small Python client that demonstrates optimistic reads and enqueue semantics.
- adapters/tool-proxy/streaming-relay.ts: TypeScript websocket relay and proxy adapter used by the playbook.
- adapters/tool-proxy/README.md: integration notes for connecting external tools (auth patterns, backpressure).
- docs/snippets/deferred-indexing.md: docs site snippet with recommended config flags for Redwood Optimize (batch/kv-cache hints).
- tests/integration/deferred_index_smoke.test.ts: basic e2e smoke tests for local run.
- examples/workflows/deferred-index-github-actions.yml: simple GH action to exercise the local smoke test.

Notable behaviors and examples:
- The playbook intentionally demonstrates an 'optimistic serve' where new documents are queryable from a short-lived prefix cache before a full index merge completes; this is annotated with caveats in the README.
- The streaming-relay supports an ACK/receipt flow and a fallback HTTP webhook mode for environments without websockets.
- docs/snippets/deferred-indexing.md includes recommended Redwood API routing policy snippets to route low-latency reads to cached shards while background merges are underway.

Interleaved activation checkpointing and buffer coalescing to cut peak GPU workspace

Motivation: In production we observed recurring OOMs and large transient workspace peaks for long-sequence (>=4k) generation and KV-heavy batched workloads. Previous work focused on per-layer checkpointing and arena sizing; this PR targets three complementary levers to reduce peak GPU footprint without changing numeric behavior: 1) interleaved activation checkpointing that staggers recompute windows to shrink concurrent activation sets, 2) scratch buffer coalescing that merges short-lived per-op scratch allocations into a reusable sub-arena, and 3) scheduler hints that adjust continuous-batching flush thresholds to avoid pathological peak overlaps with KV cache refill phases.

Summary of changes (commits):
- commit 1: implement interleaved checkpoint planner and unit tests (planner/ckpt_planner.{cpp,h}, tests/ckpt_planner_tests.cpp)
- commit 2: introduce coalesced scratch allocator and sub-arena lifecycle (runtime/scratch_coalesce.{cpp,h}, runtime/sub_arena.{cpp,h})
- commit 3: hook allocator into kernel queue; add allocator metrics and tracing points (runtime/kernel_queue.cpp, observability/metrics_registry.cpp)

- Scratch coalescing introduces a short-lived sub-arena that consolidates fast scratch allocations from kernels that previously carved many small temporary buffers. Introduce header probing + prefetch bridge for streaming tool-calls and structured-output OpenAI-compat adapter

Motivation: customers reported intermittent failures when using browser-based streaming tool/function-calls behind proxies or CDNs that drop or re-order custom auth headers. The failures manifest as aborted streaming sessions or tool-call rejections during the initial tool metadata exchange. This PR adds a small, backward-compatible probe-and-bridge flow that reduces the likelihood of mid-stream failures and clarifies the header contract for OpenAI-compatible clients.

Design summary: we introduce an OPTIONS-based 'header-probe' that the client MAY issue prior to establishing the streaming WebSocket/HTTP stream. When supported, the probe negotiates which of the following headers will be preserved across the proxy path: X-Redwood-Signed-Nonce, X-Project-Key, X-Org-Scoped-Token. If the probe detects header preservation issues, the client can use the 'prefetch bridge' endpoint (/_prefetch_bridge) which accepts the signed nonce via a short-lived POST and returns a one-time session token tied to the tool-call handshake. The session token is compatible with existing signing semantics and is safe to include in standard Authorization headers and cookie-based proxies.

Compatibility layer: to preserve OpenAI-compatibility we add a structured-output adapter for tool and function call handshakes. The adapter maps legacy header names (openai-internal-* and api-key variations) to our canonical headers, and normalizes nonce/signature frames emitted in stream chunks so older clients and proxies that split text frames do not lose signature context.

- add header-probe controller and OPTIONS handler
- add /_prefetch_bridge token issuance handler (short-lived, single-use tokens)

- end-to-end tests simulating proxies that strip headers; unit tests for signature chaining
- docs and migration notes for the compat adapter

Context and motivation: This PR brings a cross-SDK convergence change set across Python, TypeScript, and Go SDKs to standardize backoff semantics, emit richer retry/streaming telemetry events, and smooth a few ergonomic rough edges in stream consumers.

The goal is parity for default retry behavior (exponential+jitter with an optional max_elapsed config), clearer telemetry for upstream callers to reason about retries and resumptions, and small UX improvements that avoid surprising edge cases observed in recent incidents.

Non-goals: changing server-side protocol or adding new server features.

Implementation notes and trade-offs: to keep runtime overhead minimal, telemetry events are emitted through the existing metrics bridge with a new compact schema (no heavy JSON payloads) and a per-client sampling rate controlled by client options.

atomic release staging, Helm preflight hooks, and compressed release manifests for safer private-installer rollouts

Motivation: private on‑prem/VPC upgrades require greater atomicity and preflight validation to avoid partial rollouts and long rollback windows.

This PR introduces a small release staging layer, Helm preflight hooks (pre-install/pre-upgrade/validate), and a compact compression/packing step for release manifests and provenance files so that the installer can stage an entire release snapshot atomically and validate it before switching the live release pointer.

Design summary: 1) release-stager: an ephemeral staging area in S3/GCS with an atomic 'active' pointer object; publish pipeline uploads a packed, signed archive and a JSON index; after successful post-signature validations the pipeline atomically swaps a symlink-style object (bucket key replace) to make the new release active; 2) manifest packing: index_pack.go creates deterministic tar stream, zstd compresses blobs with level 3 for speed, and the pack includes SHA256 provenance metadata for each entry to simplify verification during installs; 3) Helm preflight hooks: small Helm hooks run before install/upgrade to validate node resources, image accessibility, KMS availability, and required CRDs; failures are surfaced early and abort the Helm transaction; 4) installer/rollback: upgrade tool gains a two-phase apply with an automatic dry-run validation and a deterministic rollback plan derived from the staged index so rollbacks are fast and do not rely on ad-hoc heuristics.

CI changes: new pipeline job ci/pipelines/release-stager.yml validates packing/compression, runs signature verification, and performs a smoke deploy to minikube in under 6 minutes.

Security: signing routine ensures reproducible tar order before cosign signing and inserts a small attestation with build-info and builder git-ref.

Backwards compatibility: published archives include both packed zstd artifact and legacy uncompressed blobs to allow older private-installer clients to continue fetching if necessary; rollout plan includes a two-week dual-read window before deprecating legacy path.

Testing: unit tests for packer and signature validator, integration tests for staged swap and Helm preflight, and manual canary in a staging VPC.

Rollout: merge -> pipeline produces staged artifact -> run canary promotion job -> after 24h and monitoring approval, auto-swap active pointer for production.

Introduce telemetry-gradient and cost shingle inspector for prompt-shape drift detection

Motivation: We see recurring low-signal cost regressions tied to prompt-shape shifts (different prompt lengths / role-token mixes). Existing token-level cost metrics show totals but do not surface subtle distributional drift across segments of the prompt. This PR introduces two complementary pieces: 1) a telemetry-gradient metric that tracks per-invocation changes in token-cost density across prompt segments (head/mid/tail) so we can detect gradual drift; 2) a 'cost shingle inspector' abstraction that slices invocations into fixed-size token shingles, computes lightweight histograms, and emits compact sketches for downstream aggregation and dashboarding.

Goals: - Detect prompt-shape drift earlier without full trace sampling. - Provide actionable panels in the Console to show which prompt segments and model stages (embedding/encode/generate) are driving cost changes. - Add tuned alerts for gradual drift (low-amplitude, long-window) and a higher-sensitivity alert for sudden spike in tail-cost.

Summary of changes: - telemetry/gradient: new metric generator in the observability pipeline. Computes per-invocation gradients between head/mid/tail cost densities and emits incrementally aggregated counters and sketches. - telemetry/shingle: shingle extractor that emits token-shingle sketches (count-min + percentile sketch) keyed by route + prompt-shape-bucket. Light-weight, safe for high QPS. - console/dashboards: new "Prompt Shape Drift" dashboard with:  * Shingle heatmap (fractional cost per shingle)  * Gradient trend lines (head vs tail)  * Attribution panels (by model stage and kernel) - alerts/rotation: new alert rules and suppression windows to avoid noisy alerts for stable seasonal prompts. - tests: unit tests for shingle extractor, integration test harness (synthetic replay) to validate drift detection and alert thresholds.

Backwards compatibility: instrumentation tags are additive; feature can be controlled by runtime flag telemetry.shingle.enabled=false for on-prem.

Rollout plan: - Stage 1: feature flag off in prod; enable for canary tenants (5%) with verbose sampling. - Stage 2: increase to 25% and enable dashboard ingestion. - Stage 3: global rollout with tuned alerting and canary auto-disable if cost overhead exceeds 1.5%.

introduce-reservoir-based-decentralized-scale-synthesizer

Motivation: production fleets see many short-lived microbursts from tenant traffic patterns which cause oscillatory autoscaling and wasted headroom.

This PR implements a lightweight reservoir-based "decentralized scale synthesizer" that runs alongside the existing autoscaler to smooth short spikes while preserving throughput guarantees and predictable tail latency.

Design summary: 1) each node maintains a small local reservoir credit accounting window that decays over time and is topped up by observed idle capacity; 2) the synthesizer aggregates ephemeral credits across replicas via a gossip-style delta protocol to create a soft, decentralized pool without a central control plane lock; 3) scaling decisions use a two-stage policy: local fast-path uses reservoir credits to accept short bursts without triggering scale-up, while the slow-path falls back to the cluster autoscaler when sustained demand exceeds reservoir thresholds.

Key properties: bounded amplification (reservoir caps per-tenant and per-node), graceful decay to avoid persistent overcommit, and deterministic backoff in preemption scenarios.

Introduce hierarchical smoke-sampler and late-fail attenuator CI hook

Motivation: intermittent prompt-set failures (spikes driven by small cohorts) are causing noisy CI alerts and unnecessary rollbacks.

Summary: Introduces a shared KMS client abstraction used across control-plane + data-plane services to standardize timeouts, retries/backoff, and error mapping. The current KMS call sites implement timeouts inconsistently (or not at all) and several retry policies amplify load during provider-side latency spikes, which contributed to elevated 5xx during throttling events.

Key goals: - Make KMS dependency behavior predictable (bounded latency, bounded retries) - Provide a canonical error taxonomy for downstream policy (circuit breaker + degrade-mode followups) - Improve observability: metrics + structured log fields to enable on-call triage

Add dead-letter queue + guarded replay CLI for failed export batches

Summary: This PR introduces a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for audit export batches that fail delivery after exhausting retries, and adds an operator-facing replay tool with guardrails.

This is a reliability/safety feature for the SIEM-ready audit export beta (Splunk HEC / Datadog Logs / S3) to ensure we never silently drop events while still protecting the platform and customers from accidental replay storms.

Context / Motivation: During downstream outages (e.g., sustained 429s from Splunk HEC or 403s from mis-scoped Datadog keys), the exporter currently retries with backoff and then surfaces a per-destination error.

Without DLQ persistence we risk either (a) losing batches on process/queue churn or (b) having no safe operational path to replay specific failures once a customer fixes credentials/quotas.

ENG-5164 calls for a DLQ + replay tooling with explicit operator controls.

Design highlights: (1) DLQ record model: When a batch hits max_delivery_attempts OR we detect a non-retryable adapter error, we persist a DLQ record keyed by (tenant_id, export_config_id, checkpoint_range) and store the batch payload (newline-delimited JSON events) in object storage under a structured prefix.

DLQ record includes: dlq_id, created_at, tenant_id, export_config_id, destination_type, reason_code, reason_detail (redacted), first_event_ts, last_event_ts, event_count, byte_size, last_attempt_at, attempt_count, and a payload_ref. (2) At-least-once compatibility: Replays may cause duplicate deliveries.

We intentionally do not attempt exactly-once; downstream should dedup using event_id (per ADR on delivery semantics).

Replay CLI logs a reminder and requires an explicit --ack-duplicates flag. (3) Operator replay CLI: Adds bin/audit-exporter-replay (Go) to list DLQ items and replay in a controlled fashion.

Replay CLI logs a reminder and requires an explicit --ack-duplicates flag. (3) Operator replay CLI: Adds bin/audit-exporter-replay (Go) to list DLQ items and replay in a controlled fashion.

Guardrails include: required --tenant-id and --export-config-id; default is dry-run; interactive confirmation unless --yes is provided; bounded selection via --since/--until and --max-items; token-bucket rate limiting (--max-events-per-minute) to avoid spiking adapters; refuses to replay if export config is disabled OR if exporter feature flag is off for that tenant (unless --override-feature-flag is provided, which is restricted to on-call breakglass role). (4) Safety checks: Replay validates destination configuration hash matches the DLQ record by default (prevents replaying old payloads into a newly re-pointed sink).

Can be overridden with --ignore-config-hash-mismatch for incident response, but emits a prominent warning. (5) Redaction: DLQ reason_detail is run through the same redaction helper used by adapter logs to avoid accidentally persisting tokens/keys/PII.

Payloads contain audit events only (already subject to audit schema/PII policy); we do not include request/response bodies. (6) Observability: Adds metrics: audit_exporter_dlq_enqueued_total{tenant_id_hash,destination_type,reason_code}, audit_exporter_dlq_backlog_items{destination_type}, audit_exporter_dlq_backlog_events{destination_type}, audit_exporter_dlq_replay_total{result}, and audit_exporter_dlq_replay_latency_seconds.

Also adds structured logs for DLQ enqueue and replay runs (with correlation_id).

User-visible / Ops workflow: - When an adapter can’t deliver a batch and we exceed retry limits, exporter transitions the batch to DLQ and advances the live pipeline checkpoint to prevent system-wide backpressure. - On-call or Support can instruct customer to fix auth/limits, then run replay for the impacted tenant/config/time window. - Replay is incremental and rate-limited; any failures during replay are re-DLQ’d with a new reason_code (replay_failed_*).

Responses protocol adapter: stable fragment reassembly, toolcall boundaries, and seed handoff for OpenAI compatibility

Motivation: New OpenAI Responses variants expose streaming fragmentation semantics, RNG/seed hints, and richer metadata that must be faithfully represented in Redwood's Responses compatibility layer.

Without an adapter, hosted customers see reordering and truncated toolcall boundaries in streamed responses and cannot reproduce outputs when a seed is provided.

This PR implements a protocol adapter that stabilizes fragment reassembly, preserves explicit tool/function-call boundary markers in the stream, and forwards RNG/seed hints plus metadata passthrough to the sampling layer.

Design highlights: 1) Introduce lightweight fragment framing (frag_id, seq, final_flag) on the bridge to detect out-of-order chunks and perform deterministic reassembly with minimal buffering.

5) Fail-open fallback: when fragment integrity cannot be verified within a configurable timeout, the adapter falls back to per-chunk best-effort delivery and flags the event in logs/metrics.

introduce slab-grafting reclaimer and spill-rate cap to reduce KV cache fragmentation and spill storms

Motivation: In high-concurrency tenant workloads we continue to see transient spill storms driven by large numbers of small, fragmented slot allocations.

These storms increase peak GPU memory usage and cause cascading evictions that harm latency.

This PR introduces two orthogonal mitigations: (1) a slab-grafting reclaimer that coalesces adjacent free slots into larger usable extents with low CPU overhead, and (2) a spill-rate cap controller that rate-limits and smooths background spill operations to avoid sudden IO spikes.

Design: slab-grafting is implemented as a background, incremental pass that scans per-shard free lists and attempts opportunistic graft operations when fragmentation score exceeds a threshold.

Grafting is lock-free with respect to normal alloc/free paths by using a CAS-based two-phase promotion that marks ranges as 'staging' before atomically linking them into larger slabs.

The spill-rate cap is a token-bucket controller in the KV spill scheduler; it enforces a soft cap on MB/sec of spill throughput and exposes a spill_smoothing_window_ms knob.

When cap is hit, the scheduler prefers reclaiming contiguous grafted slabs and defers noncritical spill tasks.

Compatibility: the grafting path is gated behind a runtime flag enable_slab_grafting and defaults off for older clusters; the spill cap has a conservative default of 128 MB/s but is tunable per-deployment and can be disabled.

Testing: unit tests validate graft correctness across races and simulated concurrent frees; a stress harness (tools/kv_stress) demonstrates a 45% reduction in maximum concurrent spill IO during mixed-read/write tenant workloads, and a 12% P99 latency improvement on the generation path in our benchmark-lab scenarios.

Rollout plan: staged canary to 10% of pods for 48h, monitor memory residency and spill_io_mbps metrics, then 50% for 24h, then global.

Related work: follows the fragmentation detection work in ENG-3983 and complements the asynchronous compactor (ENG-4620).

Known limitations: grafting is not effective for highly interleaved small live objects; in those cases we still rely on the compactor and eviction heuristics.

Safety: feature flags and conservative defaults provided; metrics to watch: kv.fragmentation_score, kv.graft_ops, kv.spill_mbps, kv.eviction_count.

runtime: make optimization config applier idempotent + retry-safe (partial rollout safeguards)

Context: As part of Safe apply + rollback for Optimization Configs, the control plane will issue apply operations that may be retried (network timeouts, controller restarts) and can be delivered out-of-order relative to worker restarts and shard movement. Prior implementation applied configs as a best-effort "set current" and would re-run side effects on every delivery (cache invalidation, batcher reinit), which increased tail latency and could leave mixed worker states during partial rollout. This PR makes the runtime Optimization Config applier idempotent and resilient to retries, and adds explicit safeguards for partial rollout states.

What changed: 1) Introduced apply_operation_id and deterministic apply keying. The runtime now consumes ApplyOptimizationConfig(scope, version, apply_operation_id, reason) and records a durable ApplyRecord per (scope, version). If the same apply_operation_id is delivered again, the operation is treated as a no-op after verifying the recorded checksum. 2) Added a small durable state store (RuntimeOptimizationConfigState) to persist last_desired_version, last_applied_version, last_apply_operation_id, and an apply_status enum (PENDING/APPLIED/FAILED). This survives worker restarts and prevents "double apply" side effects after process crashes. 3) Side-effect gating: cache invalidation and batch scheduler resets now run only on transition from one applied version to another, and are skipped on idempotent retries. 4) Partial rollout safeguards: if a worker receives an apply for an older version than its recorded desired_version, it will reject it with a conflict response unless reason=ROLLBACK (explicit rollback) or allow_downgrade=true from control plane. This prevents late/stale apply messages from reintroducing a regressed version mid-rollout. 5) Repair behavior: if apply_status is FAILED for the same (scope, version) and the controller retries with a new apply_operation_id, the runtime will re-attempt apply (previously a failed apply could wedge workers until manual restart). 6) Observability: added metrics and structured logs to make retry/no-op/conflict behavior visible: optimization_config_apply_total{result=applied|noop|conflict|failed}, optimization_config_apply_duration_ms, and optimization_config_state_gauge{state}. All are tagged with tenant/model/region/config_version/apply_operation_id (apply_operation_id only in logs to avoid high cardinality metrics).

Why this is safe: The new behavior is strictly more conservative. Duplicate deliveries become no-ops, stale messages are rejected, and only explicit rollbacks can downgrade. Persisted state ensures crashes don’t cause reapplication storms (and the associated cache flush latency spikes). Unit + integration tests cover retry ordering, crash/restart, and conflict semantics.

paged-kv: implement soft-pin block allocator and reuse heuristics to reduce fragmentation

Motivation: long-lived KV cache entries and block fragmentation were causing elevated tail latency and increased GPU memory pressure under mixed-sequence workloads.

This PR introduces a 'soft pin' block allocation strategy and stronger reuse heuristics for the paged KV block manager to reduce allocation churn and eviction storms.

Summary of changes: 1) New soft-pin concept for blocks: blocks can be marked soft-pinned when referenced by in-flight decode contexts; they are excluded from immediate eviction but eligible for reuse by same-owner contexts to avoid duplication.

2) Segregated free lists per size class with compact LRU buckets to improve reuse locality.

3) Eviction ranking that factors in last-access timestamp, owner affinity, and live-kv-count to avoid evicting hot multi-token KV pages.

4) GC/compaction path to coalesce small free fragments when fragmentation exceeds threshold.

5) Runtime knobs: kv.soft_pin_v2 (bool), kv.free_list_threshold (int), kv.compact_fraction (float).

Design notes: the soft-pin is a lightweight per-block ref-bit plus ownership tag; ownership is used only as a hint for reuse and does not bypass safety checks.

Reuse is conservative: blocks reclaimed for reuse must not have active external pointers.

Benchmarks: local microbench (mixed chat + completion load, seq distribution 8-1024) shows 10-14% reduction in p99 token-latency and ~12% throughput improvement on T4-equivalent nodes; memory overhead reduced ~6% due to less duplicated KV pages.

Rollout plan: feature gated, canary on 5% of hosted traffic, ramp to 50% after 48h if perf signals stable.

Backout: revert kv.soft_pin_v2 or set kv.free_list_threshold high.

Related work: follow-ups planned to integrate with continuous batching's slot-aware scheduling to further co-locate reuses.

Motivation: Reproducing user-facing RAG regressions that depend on network latency, index freshness, or multi-tool interactions is time-consuming.

This quickstart introduces the TimeWarp simulator — a lightweight local harness that lets engineers run deterministic, time-scaled RAG scenarios and assert structured outputs against expected contracts.

The goal is a low-friction developer loop to reproduce flaky tool-calls, evaluate output stability under synthetic delays, and run quick regressions in CI.

What this PR adds: 1) quickstarts/timewarp-simulator/README.md — end-to-end guide and expected workflows; 2) a compact TypeScript runner (runner/ts/) that drives synthetic user sessions with configurable latency/timewarp factors and replayable corpora; 3) a structured-output linter (examples/linting/structured-output-linter.py) that validates JSON/YAML responses against field-level contracts and fuzzy string expectations; 4) telemetry probes (telemetry/probes.yaml) and a CI smoke job (ci/smoke-timewarp.yml) that runs a short scenario on PRs to catch regressions; 5) docs site registration (docs/quickstarts.yml and docs/snippets/timewarp-setup.md) so quickstart appears in the docs sidebar.

Add reservoired burst-accountant and steady-window SLO profiles for Dedicated fleets

Customers observed intermittent microburst patterns that repeatedly pushed Dedicated tenants past short-term P95 latency SLAs despite healthy long-window utilization. This PR introduces a reservoired burst-accountant and a configurable steady-window SLO profile to explicitly decouple short burst allowances from steady throughput guarantees.

What this changes: added a credit reservoir model (per-tenant, per-fleet) that accrues credit when observed usage is below a configurable steady-window baseline, and draws down when short-term bursts exceed nominal throughput. Credits are persisted in the reservation ledger with TTL and soft-eviction semantics. A new steady-window SLO profile (window length, baseline qps, burn-rate caps, recovery rate) can be attached to tenant reservations and accepted by the autoscaler and admission controller. The admission controller now consults the accountant to allow transient overcommit within the credit budget, and emits telemetry so ops can see effective burst headroom and expected exhaustion times.

Why: previous autoscaling heuristics conflated short-term spike handling with long-window capacity planning, leading to noisy scale-ups and SLA flapping. The reservoir model reduces unnecessary scale churn, improves tail latency consistency, and provides an audit trail for transient overages.

Compatibility and opt-in: new behavior is gated behind the feature flag "reservoired_burst_accountant" and is enabled by default for Dedicated fleets started after the release date. Existing fleets will remain on traditional burst heuristics unless opt-in is performed via the Console or API. Backward-compatible admission paths exist: if the accountant data is unavailable, the system falls back to current conservative limits.

Testing and validation: unit tests for ledger persistence, integration tests simulating realistic burst profiles, and a small-scale canary (10 fleets) run in perf-lab. Load tests show P95 latency improvements of 12-18% on bursty workloads and reduced autoscale events by ~28%.

Rollback plan: revert feature flag (ops) to disable accountant and fall back to baseline burst limits. Post-merge tasks: telemetry dashboard, Console opt-in UI, and a follow-up PR to add a per-tenant dry-run mode that reports but does not enforce credit draws.

Introduce inference health scorer and token-cost forecast panel

Motivation: Production teams want a single, explainable signal that summarizes invocation health (latency, cost, cache-warmth, model-fallbacks) and a short-term forecast of token burn to reduce noisy alerts during predictable bursts. This PR introduces a lightweight per-invocation 'inference_health_score' (0-100) plus a token-cost forecast panel that surfaces 1h/6h/24h EWMA forecasts and a confidence band.

- Aggregation/worker: observability/pipelines/forecast_worker.go computes per-tenant EWMA forecasts for token-cost (tokens/sec and token-cost/sec) and writes forecast series to the metrics cache. perf: cross-batch dequant fusion with amortized per-token rescale for mixed-precision kernels

Motivation: Long-context workloads show fragmentation across microbatches that prevent effective dequant fusion and cause repeated dequant/rescale operations per token.

This PR introduces a cross-batch dequant fusion pass plus an amortized per-token rescale step that cooperates with the KV cache and continuous batching coordinator to reduce redundant dequant work for INT8/FP8 mixed-precision serving.\n\nSummary of changes: implemented a new CrossBatchDequanter that tracks compatible contiguous microbatch windows and emits a fused dequant operation for stacked tokens; added an AmortizedRescale operator that defers fine-grained scale adjustments until token groups exceed a stability threshold; extended the scheduler with a cross-batch affinity hint and modified the KV cache interface to expose per-layer scale metadata needed by the fused path.

Differential audit sampling + KMS call-path reconciliation for RBAC v2 operator scope

Motivation: Reduce sensitive-audit volume while preserving forensic fidelity and ensuring per-call KMS provenance for operator-scoped actions.

This PR implements a differential audit-sampling layer (route + risk aware) integrated with an end-to-end KMS call-path reconciler to ensure any sampled event carries provable KMS metadata that can be traced back to the operator credential used.

Changes include a sampling policy engine, hooks in the RBACv2 enforcer to emit sampling signals, and a background reconciler that annotates audit events with KMS proofs and retries failed attestations.

Rollout: feature gated behind runtime flag rbacv2.diff_audit_sampling; default off for enterprise accounts.

When enabled, low-risk routes use probabilistic sampling, high-risk routes (policy change, KMS key ops, operator escalation) are always retained.

The reconciler runs asynchronously and attaches kms_proof:{provider,region,key_id,nonce,signature} when available.

Add RAG mosaic authoring stubs and live-preview quickstart

Introduce a compact quickstart that demonstrates a 'mosaic' authoring pattern for RAG scenarios: template stubs, a live preview server, telemetry probes, and a devcontainer for local onboarding.
Motivation and summary: Add a lightweight quickstart that shows authors how to compose retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) scenarios using a 'mosaic' layout: small, composable step templates (retrieval, transform, tool-call, finalization) that can be arranged and previewed in real time. This is targeted at developer-first product teams who want fast iteration cycles when authoring multi-step agents and tool-calling flows. The quickstart includes: 1) starter templates for step types, 2) a tiny live-preview server that streams intermediate step outputs into a mosaic UI, 3) telemetry probes and example probes for Redwood Console, 4) a devcontainer and scripts to run locally, and 5) CI e2e smoke tests.

What changed (high-level): commits: - Add mosaic authoring templates and README (initial scaffolding) - Add live-preview server (FastAPI + SSE) and browser UI - Wire telemetry probe hooks and example telemetry config - Add devcontainer, Makefile and local-run scripts - Add CI smoke test that runs quickstart e2e in headless mode - Docs site section and short how-to guide

Changed areas/files (representative): - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/README.md (new authoring guide and examples) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/templates/*.yaml (retrieval/transform/tool/output stubs) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/live-preview/server.py (SSE endpoints + example runner) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/live-preview/static/index.html (mosaic UI) - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/devcontainer.json + .devcontainer/Dockerfile - quickstarts/rag-mosaic/telemetry/probes.yaml - .github/workflows/quickstart-e2e.yml (added smoke job) - docs/site/content/quickstarts/rag-mosaic.md (documentation and screenshots)
